messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

You don't have data2 anywhere in your script, so I'm not sure what it looks like.  Also, "Month" seems to vary across observations so you wouldn't want that as a site-level covariate.  But you could grab length and facility from the obsCovs matrix created by csvToUMF and assign them as siteCovs:

siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(Length=as.numeric(obsCovs(umf,matrices=T)$Length[,1]),
                            Facility=obsCovs(umf,matrices=T)$Facility[,1])

Now, with only 13 sites you will have problems fitting occupancy covariates.  In addition, you have only 8 detections from 1092 observations.  So this data set will undoubtedly give you problems with model fitting (null suggests psi=1 and p=0.007).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Joshua,

here are few comments:

1) it's often a good idea to standardize your covariates before analysis. You seem to have attempted to use scale( ) , but it won't take effect unless you store the results in the object.

2) If you create a named list of models, i.e., list("yd1" = yd1, "yd2" = yd2, ...), then you don't need to use the modnames argument - aictab( ) and related functions will just use the names you specified in the list.

3) What was the c-hat value you obtained from the GOF test? You want to use the value you obtained from the global model, provided c.hat > 1, but not too much (e.g., 3 or 4). You will also want to use this value to get predictions with modavgPred( ).

4) If you have models with covariates on psi or p, then it is a bit strange to compute an average value of psi or p, especially if some models with covariates have a lot of support. It would be more meaningful to compute predictions of psi or p in relation to some values of your variables of interest.

5) The whole point of multimodel inference is using the entire model set so that models with a lot of support will have the greatest contribution to your estimate. You don't need to chop down the model list, just use modavgPred( ) to make predictions using the entire model set - the models without support won't contribute to the predictions.

Hope it helps,

Marc

messages.subject: Goodness of fit for N-mixture model
messages.subject_clean: Goodness of fit for N-mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
For N-mixture models fit via unmarked::pcount, the function AICcmodavg::Nmix.gof.test provides a goodness-of-fit test  based on a Pearson chi-squared statistic, compared to a bootstrapped reference distribution.  In these respects, it is similar to AICcmodavg:mb.gof.test for occupancy models.

The Mackenzie-Bailey test for occupancy models is based on the observed and expected frequencies of entire detection histories.  This test was well studied in Mackenzie and Bailey's original paper, and I believe it was shown to have good power to detect misspecification of the detection portion of the model, and less power to detect misspecification of the occupancy portion of the model.

A glance at the source code for Nmix.gof.test suggests that it is based on the sum of the squared residuals, where each residual is the difference between observed and expected counts at each site-visit.  I have two questions:
1) Has anybody studied the behavior of this test in any detail, similar to the simulation studies of Mackenzie and Bailey?
2) It seems to me that Nmix.gof.test, based on the sum of the squared residuals for each individual site-visit, might have somewhat less power to detect misspecifications of the detection probability than does the Mackenzie-Bailey statistic for occupancy models.  Is this accurate, way off base, or unknown?
3) Does anybody have suggestions of particular discrepancy functions to use in posterior predictive checks of the goodness of fit of the N-mixture model?  Are any of these described or recommended in published literature?

An example that motivates my intuition in question 2:
Imagine that detectability was consistently lower on the first visit to each site, due to unmodeled heterogeneity in p or non-independence of visits.  Then the Mackenzie-Bailey statistic would respond strongly to the excess of detection histories beginning with zero.  But it seems to me that the Nmix.gof.test statistic would attribute this to usual sampling variance, without "noticing" that the variance is highly nonrandom with respect to the visit order.

Thanks in advance for your help, and of course thanks to the developers of unmarked and AICcmodavg!
Jacob Socolar

messages.body_plain:
Dear Rodolfo,

Go the second way ! That way, you do all at once in a single model and you know what you’re doing. Ad hoc composite analyses like the first one have lots of risks in my opinion of doing things which are suboptimal, to say the least.

A binomial mixture model (that’s the one fit using function pcount --- remember not to call a model by the name of the function or the software used to fit it) gives you all at once, in a statistical rigorous way without any ad-hockery.

You have N ~ Poisson(lambda) as the model for the latent abundance N and C ~ Binomial (N, p) as your measurement error model for the observed data C and you can add covariates in either process as you are interested in them and as they’re available in a GLM-way via a link function. Note that you have two types of abundance in this model (and in reality, too): the realized abundance at a site (N) and the expected abundance (lambda). This has been discussed in this list before (or in the sister list, HMecology).

To gauge the relationship between abundance and covariates you will not normally look at the estimated N’s for your surveyed sites (i.e., at the realized abundance) but at the expected abundance at any site given the value of some covariates. Hence, use one the predict functions and predict expected abundance for a range of values for the covariates and then plot this relationship: that shows you how covariates affect (expected) abundance.

If you want to compare the effect sizes of different covariates I am not so sure. I presume you could fit all covariates after scaling them to make them comparable and then directly compare their coefficient estimates. An alternative might be to fit the model bayesianly (e.g., in BUGS software --- then it’s clearly no longer “the pcount model”) and use ideas expressed in the paper by Qian and Shen, Ecology, 2007 (And Gelman 2005 before), to compare effect sizes of explanatory variables.  Another alternative to compare the magnitude of effects of different environmental covariates, which I think is very interesting, has been described by Beale et al. (see here http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12174/abstract). They essentially do a sensitivity analysis by disturbing the value of each covariate by a constant amount and then observe which covariate, when such noise is added, leads to the greatest change in the estimated abundance. This is especially useful if you have complex covariate relationships, e.g., polynomials, interactions, or splines.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear group,

First of all, I want to thank everyone who contributes to this group. I am new to the world of abundance estimation, and this google group and 'unmarked' have been a tremendous help!

With that said, let me embarrass myself with my question.

I am trying to use the extended DM model (Hostetler and Chandler 2015) to estimate daily shorebird abundance on a migration stopover site.
Our count data comes from 14 transects which were surveyed almost daily throughout a migration season of about two months. Surveys were done
anytime during the daylight hours and thus vary in terms of tidal cycle which is known to affect the shorebird abundance on the site.
Our goal is to account for the effects of time and tide height on the detection probability and estimate daily total abundance in the area
(summing 14 transects), so that we can ultimately identify the timing of peak migration and test for long-term shifts in the migration timing.

Since we are looking at a relatively short time window, we assume the gamma parameter represents immigration (and not birth) and the omega parameter
represents probability of an individual to stay at that site the next day (and not survival). So, we are dealing with a "super-open" population
where individuals enter/leave the population everyday. Each day is a separate sampling occasion, and we have about 60 occasions.

I tested, in this order, for the best mixture, covariates for detection, best dynamics to use, covariates for initial abundance, and covariates for immigration.
And we've been setting the gamma and omega formula to be ~1. I've attached a sample data and a sample code below.

Best model we got is as following, and includes subsite-effect on the initial abundance, effects of time and tide on the detection,
and effects of subsite and the number of weeks into the season on the immigration rate.

messages.subject_clean: Extended DM model to estimate daily abundance of an open population
messages.body_plain:
Dear Eunbi Kwon,

I like the idea of what you're trying.  pcountOpen can (often) separate local and external contributions to population growth by their different signatures in the data.  In the model you're using, gamma contributes according to what the abundance at that site was the previous day, whereas iota contributes independently of that.  They're both Poisson distributed, but the fact that one depends on the abundance at the site and the other doesn't lets the model disentangle them.

You have a good point with your second question.  I think a more logical model for your situation might be:
fm2 <-  pcountOpen(~area+transect, ~area+transect+weeks, ~1, ~timep+lowtidep+hitidep, dynamics="constant", mixture = "ZIP", pm.umf, K=350)

In this version, gamma works like iota does in the first model, and omega represents the local contribution, which in your case would represent probability of a shorebird staying at that site another day.  That seems to be a more sensible way to represent your dynamics (entry and departure).  It will take even longer to run, unfortunately.

I see some other potential issues with your code.  You have transect as a continuous covariate on lambda and iota, meaning that as transect number within an area goes up, both initial abundance and entry rate decline.  Is that what you intended, or did you mean to have transect as a categorical predictor (factor)?  Unfortunately, these models can't work with this latter approach, because you'd lose spatial replication by trying to predict abundance individually at each transect.  You might be better off leaving transect out of the predictors, unless there is a clear meaning of its effect as a continuous predictor.  Your results might also be easier to interpret if you either make area a factor or make it a traditional dummy variable (0 and 1 instead of 1 and 2).

Best,

Jeff

In the meantime if the model is the simple occupancy model (no covariates, constant probability of presence and constant detection probability, and same number of visits at all sites) and the known parameter is the detection probability, then the maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of presence is

    psi-hat = min(1,(n-n0)/(n(1-(1-p)^v))

with an estimate of the asymptotic variance of

    var(psi-hat) = (n-n0)n0/(n^3(1-(1-p)^v)^2)

when 0 < psi-hat < 1 and where n is the number of sites, v is the number of visits per site, n0 is the number of sites with no detections, and p is the known detection probability.

The potential issue, of course, is "Is the detection probability really known?"  If it's "kinda" known, then maybe a Bayesian approach with a tight prior on p would be appropriate.

(Attached is a PDF document that is typeset a bit better than the above.)

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Greetings unmarked group,

I have been using gpcount to examine variation in the abundance of marsh birds in two regions. I have data for 2-3 visits within a breeding season to about 9,000 sites over a 8 year period. Our surveys include 3 "intervals" within a count, one of which is a playback interval.
I have included different combos of covariates, such as date, date2, region, time, weather variable, etc to include in the candidate models. The first thing I did was fit a global model and examine goodness of fit stats using parboot.
For a number of species, there was a lack of fit (P>0.001). So I visually inspected the fitted and observed distributions and found that the fitted distributions appeared bimodal.
And I found out that this was caused by the overwhelming effect of the playback interval, which substantially increases p.
My original thinking was that I should include interval in the model so that I look at the effect of other variables, but I'm not sure if it is reasonable to remove it, when I know it has such as large effect. Has anybody ever had an issue like this? Any ideas to remedy the situation?
Thanks
Myles

messages.body_plain:
Hi,  I hope this isn’t too basic of a question.  I’m mostly a beginner in R, and so far have been able to answer my own questions/troubleshoot based on previously answered questions.

I have count data for several species from dependent double observer surveys.  It’s a small dataset since it was for a sideproject.  I was able to get everything to work when fitting models for the counts of all species combined, but when I try to do the same for just one species at a time, I keep getting error messages like this:

Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) :

  non-finite finite-difference value [6]

Warning message:
In gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~observer - 1 + Date + Start_Time + Time_Elapsed +  :
  Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates.

The one exception is when I run the script for the species with the most observations – all models worked for it.  The same covariates are being used for all species combined and for each separately.  Is it likely that the R script is fine, but that I simply don’t have enough observations/data for most species for this type of analysis to be appropriate?  (there were a total of 118 observations, and the observations for each species ranged from 1-55)

Thank you!  Part of my script is below:  (I left out the parts that were just formating the data to fit in the unmarkedFrame, and only included a few models)

observer <- read.csv("Obs ID2.csv")[1:3,]

observer

obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)

numPrimary <- 6

obsToY <- kronecker(diag(numPrimary), obsToY)

depDoubPiFun <- function(p) {

  M <- nrow(p)

  pi <- matrix(NA, M, 2)

  pi[,1] <- p[,1]

  pi[,2] <- p[,2]*(1-p[,1])

  return(pi)

}

all_species_umf <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y, siteCovs = NULL,

obsCovs = list(observer = observer, Date = Date_df, Start_Time = Start_Time_df, Time_Elapsed = Time_Elapsed_df,

                Ave_Temp = Ave_Temp_df, Cloud = Cloud_df, Distance = Distance_df),

          numPrimary=numPrimary, obsToY=obsToY, piFun="depDoubPiFun")

null <- gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~observer-1, data = all_species_umf, mixture = "NB", K=150)

m_DA <- gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~observer-1 + Date, data = all_species_umf, mixture = "NB", K=150)

DA_TE <- gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~observer-1 + Date+Time_Elapsed, data = all_species_umf, mixture = "NB", K=150)

All <- gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~observer-1 + Time_Elapsed + Start_Time + Ave_Temp + Cloud + Distance + Date, data = all_species_umf, mixture = "NB", K=150)

(I realize this is getting pretty complex, but when I get errors, it’s often with simpler models with only one covariate, as well as with the complex ones)
